description: How vaccines build immunity, why herd immunity matters, and how labs identify pathogens.
content_html:
Strategies to Prevent Infection

Preventing communicable diseases requires strategies that target the pathogen, the host, or the route of transmission. For plant diseases, strategies include sourcing disease-free plant material, rotating crops so pathogens cannot persist in one site, destroying infected plants to prevent spread, and using chemical or biological controls. For human diseases, strategies include vaccination, hygiene measures, sterilising wounds, contraception (for sexually transmitted infections), and restricting movement of infected individuals or animals. Each strategy has costs, benefits and risks that must be weighed, and an individual’s right to choose must be balanced against what is best for the wider population.

Key Fact

Prevention strategies for communicable diseases vary by context. For humans: vaccination, hygiene and sanitation, sterilisation of wounds, contraception (for STIs), and travel restrictions. For plants: using healthy seeds, crop rotation, polyculture, destroying infected plants, and chemical or biological pesticide use.

How Vaccination Works

A vaccine introduces a safe form of a pathogen — or parts of it — into the body. The immune system responds by producing white blood cells called lymphocytes, which make antibodies specific to the pathogen’s antigens (surface markers). Some of these lymphocytes persist in the body as memory cells.

If the real pathogen is encountered in future, the memory cells recognise its antigens immediately and mount a rapid secondary response — producing the correct antibodies much faster than a first-time immune response could. This speed means the infection is usually cleared before symptoms develop. This is immunity.

First exposure (or vaccination): the immune system takes several days to identify the antigen, activate the correct lymphocyte clone, and produce antibodies in significant quantities. During this time, the pathogen may replicate and symptoms can develop. However, memory cells are formed.

Second exposure: memory cells recognise the antigen almost immediately. Antibodies are produced rapidly, typically before any symptoms appear. The infection is controlled quickly. This is the secondary immune response — faster and stronger than the primary response, which is why vaccination with a safe form of the pathogen can protect against future infection with the real pathogen.

Herd Immunity

When a large proportion of a population is immune to a pathogen — either through vaccination or previous infection — the spread of the pathogen slows dramatically. This is called herd immunity. Immune individuals cannot pass the pathogen on, so the chain of transmission breaks before the pathogen reaches those who are not immune — including vulnerable people (such as newborns or immunocompromised individuals) who cannot receive certain vaccines.

Vaccination decisions involve weighing individual risk against collective benefit. A vaccine may carry a small risk of side effects; a person might question whether that risk is worth taking if most others around them are vaccinated and herd immunity already provides protection. However, if too many people reason this way, the proportion of immune individuals falls below the threshold needed for herd immunity, and outbreaks can follow. This is a classic tension in public health between individual rights and collective responsibility.

The likely effectiveness, benefits, risks and cost of vaccination programmes must be assessed by scientists and public health bodies. Where evidence shows benefits substantially outweigh risks across the population, vaccination is recommended. Where uptake is low, disease resurges — as has occurred with measles in some regions following misinformation about vaccine safety. Sound decisions in this area require understanding of data, scientific evidence, and how to evaluate competing claims.

Key Fact

Herd immunity works by breaking chains of transmission. When enough of the population is immune, a pathogen cannot find new hosts easily enough to spread. Vulnerable individuals (the very young, elderly, or immunocompromised) are protected indirectly because the pathogen rarely reaches them. The proportion of the population that must be immune varies by pathogen — it is generally higher for very infectious pathogens.

Identifying Pathogens in the Lab: Monoclonal Antibodies

Identifying which pathogen is causing an infection is essential for choosing the right treatment. Traditional methods include culturing samples on nutrient agar, observing colonies under a microscope, and testing sensitivity to antimicrobials. A more modern and highly specific method uses monoclonal antibodies.

First, an antigen (the target molecule) is injected into an animal, stimulating the immune system to produce antibody-producing lymphocytes. Cells producing the correct antibody are then identified and isolated. These cells are cultured to produce large quantities of identical antibodies, all of which recognise the same specific antigen. Because they come from a single clone of cells, they are called monoclonal (‘one clone’) antibodies.

Monoclonal antibodies can be used in diagnostic tests: if the target antigen is present in a sample (such as blood or urine), the antibody binds to it, producing a detectable signal. This approach is used in pregnancy tests (detecting a hormone produced in early pregnancy), in rapid diagnostic tests for certain infections, and in more sophisticated ELISA tests (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays) used in laboratories to identify pathogens or measure concentrations of substances in blood.

The high specificity of monoclonal antibodies — each antibody binds only to its precise target antigen — means diagnostic tests using them are more accurate and can produce results faster than traditional culture methods. This matters when rapid diagnosis allows quicker treatment decisions and reduces the spread of infections while a patient waits for results. New technologies based on monoclonal antibodies continue to be developed, with the potential to improve diagnosis of a wide range of conditions.
exam_tip_html: For vaccination questions, make sure you can describe both what a vaccine contains (a safe form of the pathogen) and how it confers immunity (stimulating antibody production and forming memory cells). Do not confuse the primary immune response (slow, first time) with the secondary immune response (fast, due to memory cells). For monoclonal antibody production, you must be able to describe the steps in sequence: antigen injected into animal → antibody-producing cells taken and selected → cells cultured to produce identical antibodies. On evaluate questions about vaccination, always weigh individual risk against collective (herd immunity) benefit — do not just list one side.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vaccines contain a safe form of a pathogen. They stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing disease. When the real pathogen is encountered later, memory cells enable a rapid secondary response, preventing illness.
  • Herd immunity protects vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated. If enough of the population is immune, chains of transmission break and outbreaks are prevented. Individual decisions about vaccination affect collective protection.
  • Monoclonal antibodies are produced by culturing cloned immune cells; all antibodies produced are identical and specific to one antigen. They are used in highly specific diagnostic tests (including ELISA) to identify pathogens rapidly and accurately.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vaccination protects an individual from a communicable disease.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: vaccine contains safe form of the pathogen (dead/weakened/parts); stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies specific to the pathogen's antigens; memory cells are formed; if real pathogen encountered, rapid secondary response produces antibodies quickly before symptoms develop; individual is protected. Secure: three of four points present and linked. Developing: two points present; mechanism partially explained. Emerging: states vaccine prevents disease without explaining the immunological mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a large proportion of the population needs to be vaccinated for herd immunity to be effective.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: if enough people are immune, pathogen cannot find susceptible hosts to spread between; chains of transmission break before the pathogen reaches unvaccinated individuals; vulnerable people who cannot be vaccinated are indirectly protected. Secure: links proportion vaccinated to reduced transmission and protection of vulnerable; one point vague. Developing: states more vaccinated = less spread without explaining mechanism. Emerging: vague statement about herd immunity without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A new rapid diagnostic test uses monoclonal antibodies to detect a bacterial antigen in a blood sample. Evaluate the advantages of this approach compared with traditional bacterial culture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: monoclonal antibodies are highly specific (only bind to the target antigen, reducing false positives); rapid result time compared to days needed for culture; can be used in a clinical setting without specialist microbiology lab; limitation: may only detect one specific pathogen so a negative result does not rule out other infections; traditional culture allows antibiotic sensitivity testing which the antibody test does not; overall evaluation — antibody test faster and highly specific but culture provides more information. Secure: advantages and at least one limitation clearly compared; conclusion present. Developing: advantages stated but limited comparison with culture; no real evaluation. Emerging: describes monoclonal antibodies without comparing to culture or evaluating.

practice_questions.text: Describe the steps involved in producing monoclonal antibodies for use in a diagnostic test.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: antigen injected into an animal to stimulate immune response; antibody-producing cells taken from the animal; cells producing the correct antibody are selected; these cells are cultured to produce large quantities of identical antibodies all recognising the same antigen. Steps in order, all four present. Secure: three steps correct. Developing: two steps described; sequence not fully correct. Emerging: general reference to antibodies being produced without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: A parent is deciding whether to vaccinate their child against a common disease. The child is healthy and many children in the class are already vaccinated. Using ideas about risk, benefit and decision-making, discuss the factors the parent should consider.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefits of vaccination (protection for child, memory cells, rapid response if infected); risks of vaccine (minor side effects, rare adverse reactions); herd immunity argument (most classmates immune, so risk to unvaccinated child is currently lower); but if too many parents reason this way herd immunity breaks down and disease resurges; individual right to decide vs societal responsibility; role of evidence and expert guidance; balanced conclusion with reference to weighing probability of harm (disease) versus probability and severity of vaccine side effects. Secure: benefits and risks addressed; herd immunity logic included; some weighing and conclusion. Developing: benefits and risks listed without weighing; herd immunity mentioned but not developed. Emerging: one-sided answer focusing only on vaccine risks or only on benefits.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between the primary and secondary immune responses.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: primary is slower / takes several days to produce significant antibody levels; secondary is faster / antibodies produced almost immediately due to memory cells. Two clear differences stated. Secure: one difference fully explained and one partially. Developing: one difference correctly stated. Emerging: vague reference to body recognising pathogen again without specifying what differs.

knowledge_checks.q: What do memory cells do when the body encounters a pathogen it has been vaccinated against?
options: They produce toxins to destroy the pathogen
They enable a rapid secondary immune response by producing antibodies quickly
They alert the skin to form a physical barrier
They release stomach acid to neutralise the pathogen

knowledge_checks.q: Monoclonal antibodies are described as 'specific'. This means they:
options: Work against all types of pathogen
Only recognise and bind to one particular antigen
Are produced faster than normal antibodies
Can destroy bacteria without immune cell involvement

knowledge_checks.q: Herd immunity protects vulnerable individuals because, when enough of the population is immune, chains of _____ break.
A vaccine contains a safe form of a pathogen that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies without causing _____.
Match each term to its correct description.
right: Long-lived lymphocyte enabling rapid secondary immune response
Protein on pathogen surface that triggers immune response
Protein produced by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen

flashcard_questions.a: A safe form of a pathogen — dead, weakened, or parts of it.
Long-lived lymphocytes that remain after vaccination and enable rapid secondary immune responses.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the secondary immune response faster than the primary response?
flashcard_questions.a: Memory cells recognise the antigen immediately and produce antibodies rapidly.
A molecule on the surface of a pathogen recognised as foreign by the immune system.
Indirect protection of unvaccinated individuals when enough of the population is immune to break chains of transmission.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are monoclonal antibodies described as specific?
flashcard_questions.a: Each monoclonal antibody only recognises and binds to one particular antigen.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first step in producing monoclonal antibodies?
flashcard_questions.a: Injecting the target antigen into an animal to stimulate an immune response.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one use of monoclonal antibodies in diagnosis.
flashcard_questions.a: Detecting a specific antigen in a blood or urine sample using an ELISA test.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one plant disease prevention strategy.
flashcard_questions.a: Crop rotation (or: sourcing disease-free seeds, destroying infected plants, biological control).

flashcard_questions.q: What risk must be weighed when deciding whether to vaccinate the population?
flashcard_questions.a: Small risk of vaccine side effects against the larger benefit of preventing disease and maintaining herd immunity.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to herd immunity if too few people are vaccinated?
flashcard_questions.a: The threshold is not met, transmission chains are not broken, and outbreaks can occur.

glossary_terms.definition: A preparation containing a safe form of a pathogen (dead, weakened, or parts of it) that is introduced into the body to stimulate an immune response without causing disease.
Proteins produced by lymphocytes that are specific to a particular antigen on a pathogen. They bind to the antigen to disable or tag the pathogen for destruction.
Molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of a pathogen that are recognised as foreign by the immune system and trigger an immune response.
Long-lived lymphocytes that remain in the body after an infection or vaccination and enable a rapid immune response if the same pathogen is encountered again.

The indirect protection that occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of a population has become immune to an infection, so reducing the spread of the pathogen and protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
Antibodies produced in the laboratory from cloned immune cells, all of which recognise the same specific antigen. Used in diagnostic tests and medical treatments.
